_comment: Editorial introductions rendered at the top of each document partial. Edit freely; re-run `node scripts/build-faith-received.mjs` to regenerate the partials. Voice: brief, scholarly, pastorally serious. No em dashes (use a regular dash with spaces).
polanus-syntagma: Amandus Polanus von Polansdorf (1561-1610) wrote the Syntagma Theologiae Christianae as a working textbook for the Reformed academy at Basel; the first folio appeared in 1609, the definitive Hanau edition in 1615. It is the first fully systematic Reformed scholastic theology, organised on the bifurcating Ramist method: every locus is divided into two, then two again, until the entire matter of dogmatics has been distributed across ten books. Wollebius, Maccovius, Gomarus and the wider Dutch Reformed tradition all leaned on it. This English edition is Stiven Peter's translation of the SCTA diplomatic transcription of the 1615 Hanau folio, paired with a facing Latin-English verification edition and released, like the source, under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. As of this edition only Liber I (De Theologiae Principiis - on the principles of theology) is available; the remaining nine books will be added as the translation progresses.
apostles-creed: The Apostles' Creed is the earliest and most concise statement of the Christian faith - a baptismal confession that took shape over the second through fourth centuries as the Church taught new converts what to believe and what to renounce. It carries the structure of a triune confession: the Father who creates, the Son who redeems, the Spirit who sustains. To recite it is to enter the long company of Christians who have answered the question, "What do you believe?" with these same words.
nicene-creed: The Nicene Creed was hammered out at the councils of Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 to answer the most pressing question of the early Church: who exactly is Jesus of Nazareth? Against Arius, who taught that the Son was a creature, the Council confessed the Son as homoousios - of the same substance as the Father, true God from true God. The Creed remains the most widely received doctrinal standard in Christendom, recited by Catholic, Orthodox, and most Protestant churches alike.
chalcedonian: At the Council of Chalcedon in 451, the Church faced its second great Christological crisis: not whether the Son was fully God, but how he could be both fully God and fully human in one person. The Chalcedonian Definition gives the answer in four adverbs - without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Christ is one and the same, made known in two natures. This is the language Christianity has used ever since to confess the Incarnation.
athanasian: The Athanasian Creed, despite its name, was not written by Athanasius but emerged from the Latin West sometime between the fifth and sixth centuries. It is the longest and most thorough of the ecumenical creeds, repeating its central confession with the precision of a song so it cannot be misheard: the Trinity in Unity, the Unity in Trinity. Its sharp anathemas - "this is the catholic faith, which except a man believe faithfully, he cannot be saved" - were meant to be read aloud in worship.
didache: The Didache, or "Teaching of the Twelve Apostles," is the earliest surviving Christian church order outside the New Testament - written sometime between the late first and early second century. It is a manual: how to live the Way of Life, how to be baptized, how to celebrate the Eucharist, how to recognize true and false teachers. To read it is to overhear the Church's earliest pastoral instincts, the Way of Life and the Way of Death set side by side without commentary.
diognetus: The Letter to Diognetus is a second- or third-century Christian apology to a pagan inquirer, asking why Christians live as they do. The author - unknown to us - answers with one of the most striking descriptions of the Christian's place in the world ever written: Christians dwell in the world as the soul dwells in the body, holding it together precisely because they love it without belonging to it. The letter is often anthologized as a foundational document of Christian political theology.
augsburg: The Augsburg Confession, presented to Emperor Charles V in 1530 by the Lutheran electors, is the founding doctrinal document of the Protestant Reformation. Drafted by Philip Melanchthon under Luther's review, it sets out the Reformation's case in 28 articles: justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, the right administration of the sacraments. The Confession was a peace offering as much as a manifesto, hoping the Roman party would recognize Lutheran teaching as an internal reform of the catholic Church.
belgic: The Belgic Confession was written in 1561 by Guido de Brès, a Reformed pastor preaching in the Spanish-occupied Low Countries. He composed it under threat of execution, hoping to persuade the Catholic authorities that the Reformed faith was not sedition but the catholic Christian faith. The Confession was thrown over the wall of the King of Spain's castle at Tournai shortly after it was written. Two years later, de Brès was hanged for it.
thirty-nine-articles: The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion were finalized in 1571 to define the doctrinal position of the Church of England between the Roman and Reformed extremes after the upheaval of the English Reformation. They are deliberately moderate and broadly Protestant - Reformed in their doctrine of grace, churchly in their sacramental theology, open enough to hold together a national church. They remain the doctrinal standard of the Anglican Communion.
1689: The Second London Baptist Confession, often called the 1689, is the most thorough confession of the Reformed Baptist tradition. Its English drafters worked closely from the Westminster Confession, copying Westminster's language wherever they agreed and rewriting only on baptism, the church, and civil government. The result is a document that sits inside the Reformed family while staking out a particular polity: believer's baptism, congregational church order, religious liberty under the civil magistrate.
heidelberg: The Heidelberg Catechism was written in 1563 for the churches of the Palatinate by Zacharias Ursinus and Caspar Olevianus, on commission from the elector Frederick III. It asks the reader a single, enormous question: "What is your only comfort, in life and in death?" The 128 questions that follow are an exposition of that answer - a map of the Christian life from misery through deliverance into gratitude, organized into 52 Lord's Days for weekly preaching. Four and a half centuries later, it remains one of the warmest and most pastoral documents the Reformation produced.
westminster-shorter: The Westminster Shorter Catechism was finalized in 1647 by the Westminster Assembly, an English parliamentary body convened to bring the worship and doctrine of the Church of England into conformity with Reformed practice. Its 107 questions and answers were written for children and new converts, but its precision is such that adults still find it the surest summary of Reformed doctrine in English. It opens with one of the most-quoted lines in Protestant history: man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.
westminster-larger: The Westminster Larger Catechism, finalized alongside the Shorter in 1647, was written for the pulpit rather than the home - an exposition of the same doctrine in 196 questions, with longer answers, fuller scripture proofs, and more careful distinctions. Where the Shorter Catechism gives a definition, the Larger walks through implications. Where the Shorter answers in a sentence, the Larger answers in a paragraph. Together they remain the standards of the Reformed Presbyterian tradition.
lausanne: The Lausanne Covenant was issued by the 1974 International Congress on World Evangelization, convened in Lausanne by Billy Graham and John Stott. Its 15 articles are the founding statement of contemporary global evangelicalism - a confession of biblical authority, a call to evangelism inseparable from social concern, and an explicit repentance for the cultural captivity of Western missions. It remains the closest thing modern evangelical Protestantism has to an ecumenical creed.
ninety-five-theses: On October 31, 1517, Martin Luther - then an Augustinian monk and professor at Wittenberg - posted 95 propositions challenging the sale of indulgences. He intended a scholarly disputation; he ignited the Protestant Reformation. The Theses themselves are not yet the mature Lutheran Reformation: they are a young theologian's pastoral protest against a particular abuse, working out the deeper logic of repentance and the gospel as he writes.
edwards-resolutions: Jonathan Edwards composed his Resolutions between 1722 and 1723, while he was in his late teens and early twenties. They are private - meant to be re-read once a week, "remembering," as he put it, "to be sensible that I am unable to do anything without God's help." They give us a window into the most rigorous Reformed mind New England ever produced as that mind was forming itself: terrifyingly disciplined, candidly self-aware, oriented entirely toward the glory of God.
athanasius-incarnation: Athanasius wrote On the Incarnation around 318, before the Council of Nicaea, before he was made Bishop of Alexandria, before the long years of exile. It is his classic defense of why God became man - to undo death, restore the image, and conquer the corruption introduced into the human race by sin. C.S. Lewis, who wrote the introduction to the standard English translation, called it "a masterpiece" by "a great theologian."
augustine-confessions: Augustine wrote the Confessions in his early forties, between 397 and 400, a decade after his conversion. They are the first great Western autobiography - an extended meditation on memory, time, sin, grace, and the restless heart that finds no rest until it rests in God. The book is addressed entirely to God in the second person; the reader is overhearing a conversation between a great soul and his Maker.
calvin-institutes: John Calvin published the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1536, when he was 26, as a small handbook for French Protestants suffering under persecution. He revised and expanded it for the rest of his life; the final 1559 edition, from which the standard modern texts descend, is the foundational systematic theology of the Reformed tradition. Calvin's structure follows the Apostles' Creed: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and the means of grace.
charnock-attributes: Stephen Charnock, an English Puritan ejected from his Anglican living in 1662, spent the last decades of his life preaching what would become the great work of his career. Published posthumously in 1682, The Existence and Attributes of God is the most thorough Puritan treatment of the divine perfections in the English language - fourteen discourses on God's existence, eternity, immutability, omnipresence, knowledge, wisdom, power, holiness, goodness, dominion, and patience. The work is intellectually demanding and pastorally devastating in equal measure.
imitation-of-christ: The Imitation of Christ, written in Latin between 1418 and 1427 and traditionally attributed to Thomas à Kempis of the Brethren of the Common Life, is the most widely read Christian devotional work after the Bible. It is a guide to the interior life - the cultivation of humility, the renunciation of self, the love of God in solitude - drawn from the Devotio Moderna tradition of late-medieval Holland. Read by Catholics and Protestants alike for six centuries, it remains a sober warning against every form of religion that does not change the heart.
rerum-novarum: Pope Leo XIII published Rerum Novarum on May 15, 1891, addressing what the title calls "new things" - the upheavals of the industrial revolution, the rise of socialism, and the condition of the working classes. The encyclical condemns both Marxist collectivism and laissez-faire capitalism, defends the right to private property, the dignity of labor, and the just wage, and is the foundational text of modern Catholic Social Teaching. Its influence on Christian social and political thought across the twentieth century is difficult to overstate.
1928-bcp: The 1928 Book of Common Prayer is the last revision of the American Prayer Book before the controversial 1979 edition that replaced it. It contains the full liturgical life of the Anglican Church: the Daily Office of Morning and Evening Prayer, the Holy Communion, the sacramental rites of Baptism, Confirmation, Matrimony, and the Visitation of the Sick, the Burial of the Dead, the Ordinal for making deacons, priests, and bishops, the Psalter in Coverdale's translation arranged for the 30-day cycle, and the prayers and thanksgivings that mark the occasions of ordinary life. The daily office preserves the structure Cranmer laid down in 1549. This edition presents the original Elizabethan English alongside a modernized reading for those who prefer contemporary language, while preserving the cadence and theology of the text.
anf-clement-corinthians: Clement's letter to the Corinthians, written around AD 96, is the earliest surviving Christian document outside the New Testament. The church at Rome writes to the church at Corinth to address a factional uprising against the presbyters. Clement appeals to the order of creation, the example of the patriarchs and apostles, and the structure of the Roman military to argue that God's people must submit to their appointed leaders. The letter reveals a church already thinking institutionally, already conscious of its responsibility for order beyond its own walls.
anf-polycarp-philippians: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and disciple of the apostle John, wrote to the Philippians sometime in the early second century in response to their request. The letter is pastoral and practical, urging faith, patience, and almsgiving while warning against the love of money. Polycarp quotes Paul and the Gospels freely, giving us one of the earliest witnesses to the formation of the New Testament canon.
anf-martyrdom-polycarp: The Martyrdom of Polycarp, written by the church at Smyrna around 155-160, is the oldest surviving account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament. Polycarp, aged 86, refuses to swear by Caesar's fortune or revile Christ. The account is theological as much as historical: the church at Smyrna reads his death as a liturgical act patterned on the passion of Christ, right down to the timing and the prayer.
anf-ignatius-epistles: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote seven letters while being transported under armed guard from Syria to Rome for execution around AD 110. The letters reveal a man burning with two desires: to preserve the unity of the churches under their bishops, and to be devoured by the beasts in the arena as a living sacrifice. His theology of the episcopate, the Eucharist, and martyrdom shaped the early church's self-understanding more than any other post-apostolic writer.
anf-martyrdom-ignatius: The Martyrdom of Ignatius narrates the arrest, journey, and execution of the bishop of Antioch in the Roman Colosseum under Emperor Trajan. Its date and historical reliability are debated, but it preserves the early church's memory of one of its most celebrated witnesses. Whether composed shortly after the events or embellished in later centuries, the text stands as testimony to the early Christian conviction that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.
anf-barnabas: The Epistle of Barnabas, written sometime between AD 70 and 132, is not a letter so much as a theological treatise cast in epistolary form. Its central argument is that the Old Testament belongs to Christians, not to Jews, because Israel never understood it rightly. The author reads the Hebrew scriptures through an allegorical lens, finding Christ and the church in every detail of the Law. The last four chapters present an early form of the Two Ways teaching also found in the Didache.
anf-papias-fragments: Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor, composed a five-volume work titled Exposition of the Oracles of the Lord around AD 95-120. The work itself is lost; what survives are fragments preserved by Irenaeus, Eusebius, and others. These fragments are invaluable: Papias reports oral traditions about the apostles, explains the origins of the Gospels of Mark and Matthew, and gives us a window into the earliest decades of the church's oral memory.
anf-hermas-shepherd: The Shepherd of Hermas was one of the most widely read Christian texts of the second century, considered scripture by some early authorities including Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria. Written in Rome, probably over several decades, it presents a series of visions, commandments, and parables delivered to a freedman named Hermas. Its central concern is whether post-baptismal sin can be forgiven, and its answer is carefully pastoral: one more chance at repentance, but only one.
anf-justin-first-apology: Justin Martyr's First Apology, addressed to Emperor Antoninus Pius around AD 155, is the most important early Christian defense of the faith. Justin was a philosopher who found in Christianity the true philosophy, and he writes as one philosopher addressing another. The Apology contains our earliest detailed descriptions of Christian worship, including the Sunday assembly, the reading of scripture, baptism, and the Eucharist.
anf-justin-second-apology: The Second Apology is a shorter, more urgent sequel to the First, prompted by the unjust execution of Christians in Rome. Justin develops his doctrine of the Logos spermatikos, the "seed-bearing Word" scattered through all humanity, arguing that whatever truth the Greek philosophers possessed they possessed because the same Word who became flesh in Christ had been at work in them. The argument would prove enormously influential for later Christian engagement with pagan thought.
anf-justin-dialogue-trypho: The Dialogue with Trypho is the longest surviving early Christian apologetic work, recording what presents itself as a two-day conversation between Justin and a learned Jewish interlocutor named Trypho. Justin argues from the Hebrew scriptures that Jesus is the promised Messiah, that the Old Covenant has been fulfilled and superseded, and that the church is the true Israel. The dialogue gives us a rare window into second-century Jewish-Christian debate, even if the format is more literary than documentary.
anf-justin-discourse-greeks: The Discourse to the Greeks is a short address attributed to Justin Martyr, though its authorship has been disputed since antiquity. It calls the Greeks to abandon their contradictory and morally degrading mythology in favor of the superior wisdom found in the Hebrew prophets and the Christian revelation.
anf-justin-hortatory: The Hortatory Address to the Greeks, attributed to Justin Martyr, argues that Moses and the Hebrew prophets are older and more reliable than the Greek poets and philosophers. The author contends that whatever truth the Greeks possessed they borrowed, knowingly or unknowingly, from the Hebrews. The work reflects the early church's strategy of establishing the antiquity of its scriptures as a mark of their authority.
anf-justin-sole-government: On the Sole Government of God is a treatise attributed to Justin Martyr that marshals the testimony of Greek poets and philosophers to argue for monotheism. The author shows that Homer, Sophocles, Pythagoras, Plato, and others all acknowledged, however dimly, a single supreme deity. The argument is simple: the best minds of Greece confirm what the Christians openly confess.
anf-irenaeus-against-heresies: Against Heresies, written around AD 180, is the most important theological work of the second century. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, exposes and refutes the elaborate mythological systems of the Gnostics, particularly the Valentinians, while building his own positive theology of creation, incarnation, and salvation. His doctrine of recapitulation, in which Christ reverses the disobedience of Adam by living a fully human life in obedience, became foundational for later Christian thought. His appeal to apostolic succession and the rule of faith established the framework by which the church would evaluate doctrine for centuries.
anf-irenaeus-fragments: These fragments survive from the lost writings of Irenaeus, preserved through quotations in later authors such as Eusebius, Maximus the Confessor, and the Syrian tradition. They supplement Against Heresies with additional reflections on creation, the soul, the interpretation of scripture, and the apostolic tradition.
anf-tatian-address: Tatian, a student of Justin Martyr, wrote his Address to the Greeks around 165-175. Where Justin sought common ground with Greek philosophy, Tatian attacks it with contempt: the Greeks, he argues, are intellectual plagiarists who stole from Moses and then corrupted what they stole. The address is fierce, learned, and deliberately provocative. Tatian later left the orthodox church for the Encratite heresy, but his apologetic was widely read and his Diatessaron, a harmony of the four Gospels, was used in the Syrian church for centuries.
anf-theophilus-autolycus: Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, wrote these three books to his pagan friend Autolycus around AD 180. They defend Christianity against the standard pagan objections: that Christians worship a God they cannot see, that their scriptures are recent and unreliable, that their cosmology is absurd. Theophilus is the first known Christian writer to use the word "Trinity" (Greek: trias) for the Godhead, and his extensive quotations from Genesis make these books an important early witness to the Christian doctrine of creation.
anf-athenagoras-plea: Athenagoras of Athens addressed his Plea for the Christians to Emperor Marcus Aurelius and his son Commodus around AD 177. It is the most philosophically sophisticated of the early apologies, refuting in turn the three standard charges against Christians: atheism, Thyestean banquets (cannibalism), and Oedipean unions (incest). Athenagoras argues for monotheism from reason, for the resurrection from the nature of the human person, and for Christian morality from the behavior of the community. His prose is elegant, his argument closely reasoned.
anf-athenagoras-resurrection: On the Resurrection of the Dead is the earliest surviving Christian treatise devoted entirely to the doctrine of bodily resurrection. Athenagoras argues philosophically, not from scripture: God has both the power and the will to raise the dead; the full human person, body and soul, must be restored for justice to be done; the purpose of human existence requires that the body share in its fulfillment. The treatise became a model for later Christian defenses of the resurrection against pagan and Gnostic denial.
anf-clement-alexandria-exhortation: The Exhortation to the Heathen is the first work in Clement of Alexandria's great trilogy, written around AD 195. Clement, a convert from paganism and head of the catechetical school at Alexandria, calls the Greeks away from the mysteries and mythology of their tradition toward the true Logos, Jesus Christ. No early Christian writer was more steeped in Greek culture or more confident that it pointed, at its best, toward the Gospel. The Exhortation is an invitation from a man who loved Homer and Plato but loved Christ more.
anf-clement-alexandria-instructor: The Instructor (Paedagogus) is the second work in Clement's trilogy, following the Exhortation. Here Christ is the divine Teacher who guides the newly baptized through the details of daily life: what to eat and drink, how to dress, how to conduct oneself at banquets, how to sleep, how to speak. The result is an extraordinary window into the social world of late second-century Alexandria and the church's early attempt to form a distinctively Christian culture. Behind every particular instruction is a single principle: the disciplined life is the free life.
anf-clement-alexandria-stromata: The Stromata ("Miscellanies" or "Tapestries") is the third and most ambitious work in Clement's trilogy, composed between 200 and 210. It is a deliberately unsystematic exploration of the relationship between Greek philosophy and Christian revelation, defending the thesis that faith and knowledge are not opposites but partners. The true Gnostic, for Clement, is not the heretic but the mature Christian who unites rigorous thought with disciplined virtue under the authority of scripture. The work's sprawling, associative structure is intentional: Clement wanted to reward the patient reader, not the skimmer.
anf-clement-alexandria-rich-man: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? is a sermon by Clement of Alexandria on Mark 10:17-31, the story of the rich young ruler. Clement argues that Jesus does not condemn wealth as such but commands the stripping away of the passions that make wealth an idol. The rich are not excluded from salvation but called to a disciplined use of their possessions for the good of others. Clement closes with the famous story of the apostle John pursuing a young man who had fallen into banditry, embracing him, and restoring him to the church.
anf-tertullian-apology: The Apology is Tertullian's most famous work, written around AD 197 as a legal brief addressed to the Roman governors of Africa. It is a vigorous defense of Christianity that turns the tables on the accusers: it is the pagans, not the Christians, who are guilty of the crimes they project onto the church. Tertullian's rhetoric is fierce, his logic precise, his contempt for injustice barely contained. The work contains some of the most quoted lines in early Christian literature.
anf-tertullian-ad-martyras: Ad Martyras is a short letter of encouragement written by Tertullian around AD 197 to Christians imprisoned and awaiting execution. He urges them to see their prison as a training ground for the spirit and their coming death as a victory, not a defeat. The letter's brevity and directness reveal Tertullian at his most pastoral, offering not theological argument but the companionship of a man who believed that the arena was the threshold of glory.
anf-tertullian-shows: The Shows (De Spectaculis), written around 197-202, argues that Christians must abstain entirely from the public spectacles: the gladiatorial games, the chariot races, the theater. Tertullian's argument is not merely moral but theological: every spectacle is rooted in idolatry, and every emotion the spectacle arouses is a passion the Christian has renounced at baptism. The treatise reveals the extraordinary pressure Roman entertainment culture placed on early Christians and the severity with which the church resisted it.
anf-tertullian-answer-jews: An Answer to the Jews, written around 197-200, argues that the Old Testament prophecies have been fulfilled in Christ and that the new covenant has superseded the old. Tertullian walks through the prophets, showing how their promises point beyond Israel to the nations. The work shares substantial material with the later and more developed Against Marcion.
anf-tertullian-on-baptism: On Baptism, written around 198-200, is the earliest surviving treatise devoted to the sacrament. Tertullian explains the institution, necessity, and effects of baptism, discusses who may administer it, and argues against a group of heretics (the Cainites and their ally Quintilla) who denied its validity. The work also contains the earliest explicit argument against the baptism of infants, a point on which Tertullian is careful but firm.
anf-tertullian-on-prayer: On Prayer is Tertullian's clause-by-clause commentary on the Lord's Prayer, followed by practical instructions on the posture, times, and customs of Christian prayer. The work reveals the liturgical life of the North African church at the turn of the third century: the hours of prayer, the kiss of peace, the stations (fasting days), the role of women in worship, the practice of kneeling and standing. Behind the practical guidance is a theology of prayer as the spiritual sacrifice that has replaced the temple cult.
anf-tertullian-on-repentance: On Repentance, written between 198 and 203, distinguishes true conversion from mere regret and discusses the church's practice of exomologesis, public penance for post-baptismal sin. Tertullian argues that genuine repentance must be visible, costly, and corporate. The treatise reflects the early church's struggle with a question that would dominate the third century: what happens when the baptized fall?
anf-tertullian-idolatry: On Idolatry, written sometime between 198 and 212, is Tertullian's most comprehensive treatment of how Christians should live in a society saturated with pagan religion. He examines one occupation and social practice after another, asking in each case whether it entangles the believer in idolatry: schoolteaching, military service, commerce, civic festivals, domestic customs. The result is a demanding vision of Christian distinctiveness that allows almost no accommodation with the surrounding culture.
anf-tertullian-prescription: The Prescription Against Heretics, written around AD 200, is one of the most important works of early Christian polemics. Tertullian borrows a concept from Roman law, the praescriptio, a legal objection that stops the case before it starts. His argument: heretics have no right to appeal to scripture, because the scriptures belong to the churches that received them from the apostles. The churches hold the apostolic tradition; the heretics are trespassers. The principle of apostolic succession as the criterion of orthodoxy finds its sharpest early expression here.
anf-tertullian-on-patience: On Patience, written between 200 and 203, is one of Tertullian's most personally revealing works. He opens by confessing that he, of all people, is the least qualified to write on patience, since he is entirely without the virtue himself. What follows is a reflection on patience as the supreme Christian virtue, grounded in God's own patience toward sinful humanity. The treatise is a rare moment of humility from the most combative writer of the early church.
anf-perpetua-felicitas: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicitas, composed around AD 203, is one of the most extraordinary documents of early Christianity. The core of the text is the prison diary of Vibia Perpetua, a young noblewoman and catechumen in Carthage, recording her visions, her father's desperate pleas, and her preparation for death. It is among the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman. The narrative of the martyrdom itself was added by an anonymous editor, possibly Tertullian. The text was read liturgically in North African churches for centuries.
anf-tertullian-against-hermogenes: Against Hermogenes, written between 200 and 206, refutes a Christian painter named Hermogenes who taught that God created the world from pre-existing matter rather than from nothing. Tertullian defends creation ex nihilo as essential to God's sovereignty, arguing that if matter is eternal and uncreated, it is a rival to God. The treatise is an important early contribution to the doctrine of creation that would become standard Christian teaching.
anf-tertullian-flesh-of-christ: On the Flesh of Christ, written between 206 and 212, defends the reality of the incarnation against Marcion, Valentinus, and all who denied that Christ took genuine human flesh. Tertullian's argument is unflinching: the Son of God was truly born, truly suffered, truly died. The famous declaration, sometimes misquoted as "I believe because it is absurd," comes from this treatise. Tertullian insists that the incarnation must be real flesh, real birth, real death, or there is no real salvation.
anf-tertullian-resurrection: On the Resurrection of the Flesh, written between 206 and 212, is Tertullian's most sustained argument for the bodily resurrection against Gnostic spiritualizers who allegorized it into a purely spiritual event. He argues from creation, incarnation, the sacraments, and scripture that the flesh is not disposable but essential to God's purposes, and will be raised, transformed, and glorified. The treatise is a powerful statement of the early church's material theology.
anf-tertullian-against-valentinians: Against the Valentinians, written between 206 and 212, is Tertullian's satirical account of the most influential Gnostic system of the second century. He follows Irenaeus closely but adds his own rhetorical flair, mocking the Valentinian mythology of aeons, pleroma, and emanations with devastating wit. The work is important both as a source for Valentinian teaching and as an example of how the early church used satire as a theological weapon.
anf-tertullian-against-marcion: Against Marcion, written in its final form between 207 and 212, is Tertullian's longest and most theologically ambitious work. Across five books he refutes the dualist theology of Marcion, who taught that the God of the Old Testament was an inferior creator-deity and that Christ came to reveal a previously unknown God of pure mercy. Tertullian defends the unity of the Creator and Redeemer, the goodness of creation, the authority of the Hebrew scriptures, and the integrity of the full biblical canon. It is his masterpiece.
anf-tertullian-soul: A Treatise on the Soul, written around AD 210, is Tertullian's philosophical and theological account of the nature, origin, and destiny of the human soul. Against Platonists who taught the soul's pre-existence and Gnostics who denied its unity with the body, Tertullian argues that the soul is corporeal (in his idiosyncratic sense), created with the body, and transmitted from parent to child through generation. The doctrine, known as traducianism, would later be taken up in modified form by Augustine in his account of original sin.
anf-tertullian-chaplet: The Chaplet (De Corona), written around AD 211, was prompted by a Christian soldier who refused to wear the military laurel wreath at a donative ceremony and was arrested for it. Tertullian uses the incident to argue a broader principle: where scripture is silent, tradition and the natural sense of the faith must guide the Christian. Customs rooted in pagan worship are to be refused, even when no explicit biblical prohibition can be cited. The treatise is also an important early source for the debate over whether Christians may serve in the military.
anf-tertullian-scorpiace: Scorpiace ("Antidote for the Scorpion's Sting"), written around 211-213, is Tertullian's defense of martyrdom against Gnostics who taught that confessing Christ unto death was unnecessary and even foolish. The scorpion's sting is the Gnostic whisper that God does not really require the sacrifice of life. Tertullian answers from scripture, from the example of Christ, and from the blood of the martyrs already shed, arguing that the willingness to die is inseparable from the confession of faith.
anf-tertullian-scapula: To Scapula, written around AD 212, is a brief open letter to the proconsul of Africa warning him against persecuting Christians. Tertullian catalogues the misfortunes that have befallen previous persecutors, appeals to the loyalty and harmlessness of the Christian community, and argues that religious coercion is contrary to both natural right and divine law. The letter is one of the earliest Christian arguments for religious liberty, though framed more as a warning than a plea.
anf-tertullian-against-praxeas: Against Praxeas, written around AD 213, is the most important pre-Nicene treatise on the Trinity. Tertullian coins the Latin formula that would become standard in the West: una substantia, tres personae, one substance, three persons. The work refutes the modalism of Praxeas, who collapsed the distinction between Father and Son, teaching that the Father himself suffered on the cross (a view Tertullian calls "patripassianism"). The treatise laid the conceptual groundwork that the Council of Nicaea and its successors would later develop.
